Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have rapidly become the backbone of modern collaborative‑filtering (CF) recommender systems because they can directly exploit the bipartite user‑item interaction graph. Early efforts such as Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering (NGCF) demonstrated that propagating embeddings over the interaction graph yields richer collaborative signals than traditional matrix‑factorization approaches, which treat users and items independently of the graph structure [S2:c5f5f179d80a3bf9b4f29750283a87eaca42e91b]. At the same time, large‑scale deployments (e.g., Pinterest) showed that graph convolutional networks can be engineered for web‑scale recommendation by combining random‑walk sampling with efficient graph convolutions, proving the practical viability of GNN‑based CF on billions of nodes [S2:6c96c2d4a3fbd572fef2d59cb856521ee1746789].

Subsequent research has focused on disentangling which architectural components truly drive performance. LightGCN revealed that the two canonical GCN operations—feature transformation and nonlinear activation—contribute little to CF accuracy; a simplified model that retains only neighborhood aggregation already matches or exceeds more complex designs [S2:3024f58826a5bce3378af94f677e8fb90cbb49e0]. Complementary to this, a linear residual GCN was proposed to alleviate the training instability caused by deep non‑linear stacks, achieving competitive results while preserving interpretability [S2:c9e432023a240b22f385cf1cc76ab75fbe084ee7]. These findings collectively suggest that the essence of GNN‑based CF lies in effective high‑order neighbor aggregation rather than deep non‑linear transformations.

Recognizing the diversity of design choices, a systematic profiling of the GNN‑CF design space was conducted to map the impact of dimensions such as aggregation functions, depth, and regularization [S2:a2a42052eb8c0dd5ee339877b37f135fdfea00bd]. This work provides practitioners with a principled way to select top‑performing configurations for new recommendation scenarios without exhaustive trial‑and‑error. Broad surveys further contextualize these advances, categorizing GNN‑based recommenders into knowledge‑aware, heterogeneous, sequential, and collaborative‑filtering families, and outlining open challenges such as scalability, cold‑start mitigation, and integration of side information [S2:a669fc2d44fe5c49116a603f10d04a353468e190][S2:1be97c1d9ace0363f8f612ca1be3d4fb33e177bb][S2:f1caab91c000da3d6e8aa9800527ab0fae41c4e1].

Empirical studies confirm the practical benefits of these design insights. A recent GNN model that explicitly models user‑preference structures outperformed matrix factorization and memory‑based CF on the MovieLens‑100k benchmark, illustrating how graph‑driven representations capture nuanced relational patterns missed by shallow methods [S2:69d4dec11c850e2266d7f5b23b4f61ff2de72ffb]. Together, the literature demonstrates that GNNs not only enhance CF accuracy through higher‑order connectivity but also provide a flexible framework for incorporating heterogeneous signals, positioning them as a cornerstone of next‑generation recommender systems [S2:f97aee2318d91d83672ce248c23f6d8ecc03bb8c].
